problem: Goal-oriented VLN agents (e.g., DUET) pick actions from history and current observations only, ignoring the long-term consequences of actions. Prior future-aware methods either imagine only single-step neighbor observations (local, reconstruction-based) or roll out a world model over many slow steps prone to distortion.
motivation: Goal-oriented VLN is essentially a search problem, and A*-style heuristics on future outcomes could make frontier selection much more efficient. A cheap, long-horizon, semantic forecast that needs no instruction-annotated data would let the agent decide better when history is insufficient (early and middle steps).
key_idea: Train a task-agnostic Q-model with Q-learning-style supervision on unlabeled random trajectories to output a Q-feature (a discounted aggregate of future node text features) per candidate action, then use a cross-modal future encoder to turn these into goal-oriented future scores that are fused with DUET's history-based scores in an A*-like way.
insight: Long-horizon future information matters: γ=0.5 beats γ=0 (one-step only) at SR 53.22 vs 51.12, and ground-truth Q-features give a large upper bound (SR 59.27, SPL 47.04 vs baseline 48.14/33.38). The Q-model alone or the future encoder alone gives little gain (Table 3 rows 2 and 3), so both are needed. The shortest-path rollout policy (SR 53.22 vs 51.29 for a random policy) and text-based rather than vision-based Q-targets (SR 48.11 for vision-based) both matter.
method: Q-feature definition: Q(T,a)=Σ_{N,t} P_π(N,t|T,a) γ^t R(N), the discounted sum of future node features, so the ground truth is computed in closed form from the scene graph without RL or instructions.

Shortest-path rollout policy: futures are restricted to shortest paths from the current node, so each future node accumulates into exactly one candidate action. This keeps the candidates' Q-features discriminative and reflects efficiency.

Q-model: a 4-layer Transformer over interleaved node features (visual + caption text, 12 headings) and action features (sin/cos), followed by candidate tokens. It is trained with MSE on random partial trajectories and is frozen afterwards.

Generalization tricks: R(N) is the CLIP text feature of BLIP/LangNav captions of the node's views (text-based prediction), plus MAE-style masked-token warm-up pre-training. Optionally extra HM3D+Gibson scenes (1,351 total, no annotations) are used for Q-training.

Future encoder (FE): a 4-layer graph transformer, same as DUET's GE, run on a graph whose candidate nodes carry Q-features and whose visited nodes carry the text features. It cross-attends to the instruction, and its logits are fused with GE and LE by softmax-weighted addition.
Progress subtasks: GE predicts traversed distance and FE predicts remaining distance-to-go (5-bin classification), which decouples history from future in the A* style g+h spirit.
Three-stage training: Q-model pre-training, then DUET-style agent pre-training (MLM, SAP, OG, MRC + progress tasks), then DAgger fine-tuning.

setting.backbone: DUET-based dual-scale graph transformer + Q-model (4-layer Transformer) + future encoder (4-layer graph transformer), CLIP-ViT/B features (trained)
setting.training_data: REVERIE/SOON train sets with DUET speaker-augmented instructions (10,466 to 30,102 pairs on REVERIE); Q-model on random trajectories from MP3D train scenes, optionally plus 800 HM3D and 491 Gibson scenes (ScaleVLN scenes, no trajectory annotations)
setting.observation: panoramic RGB (36 views) with object features, plus BLIP captions for Q-model
setting.action_space: discrete topological nav-graph viewpoints (global candidates + stop)
setting.privileged: none at test (the GT Q-feature variant is only an upper-bound ablation)

results: NavQ beats the DUET baseline on all metrics on REVERIE (val-unseen SR 53.22 vs 46.98, SPL 38.89 vs 33.73, RGSPL 27.12 vs 23.03) and on SOON, and is competitive with GOAT and VER. With extra unannotated scenes it reaches SR 54.10 (val) and 54.91 (test) on REVERIE, comparable to methods using extra annotated trajectories such as AutoVLN and ScaleVLN. It also gives smaller gains on R2R and a BEVBert backbone.
limitations: Tailored to goal-oriented, shortest-path tasks; gains on R2R are smaller, and it is unsuitable for non-shortest-path benchmarks such as RxR.
Adds about 38% parameters and slows inference (0.052s vs 0.032s per step); Q-model quality still limits it (a large gap to GT Q-features).
Limited to discrete nav-graph environments, with continuous environments left to future work; test-unseen REVERIE trails GOAT and VER on some metrics.
